new_entities.name: Provoked urine heavy-metal testing
new_entities.description: Urinary metal testing performed after administration of a chelating agent such as DMSA, DMPS, or EDTA.

edges.effect_quant: A 2013 toxicology review concluded that there is no standard, validated provoked urine test and that current evidence does not support its diagnostic use. In healthy volunteers, a DMSA loading test produced urinary mercury values similar to those sometimes used to justify toxicity narratives and even caused a serious adverse reaction in one participant.
edges.population: people undergoing chelator-challenge urinary testing for suspected heavy-metal toxicity
edges.mechanism: Chelators predictably increase urinary metal excretion after dosing, but that pharmacologic effect does not establish pathological body burden or validate challenge-test reference ranges.
edges.summary: This is a contested and weakly supported diagnostic edge. Provoked urine heavy-metal testing changes urinary excretion by design, but that does not make it a validated diagnostic tool for chronic toxicity or nonspecific symptoms.
edges.caveats: Do not interpret elevated post-chelator urine values against unprovoked reference ranges. The stronger toxicology literature is cautionary, not supportive.

evidence.notes: Recommendations for provoked challenge urine testing.

evidence.citation: Archbold GP et al 2004 Ann Clin Biochem
evidence.notes: Dimercaptosuccinic acid loading test for assessing mercury burden in healthy individuals.

evidence.citation: Goldberg DM et al 1970 J Clin Pathol
evidence.notes: Measurement of mercury in human urine.
